easy.title: The 2007 Estonia Cyberattacks
easy.text: In April 2007, Estonia suffered a massive wave of cyberattacks against banks, media, and government sites. What major NATO institution was later established in Tallinn as a direct result?
options: The NATO Space Command
The NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE)
The European Central Cyber Bank
The Baltic Hardware Security Agency

easy.title: WannaCry (2017)
easy.text: WannaCry paralyzed hospitals in the UK (NHS), Telefónica in Spain, and train displays in Germany. What type of malware was WannaCry?
options: Spyware
Adware
Ransomware
Keylogger

easy.title: Operation Stuxnet (2010)
easy.text: Stuxnet is famous for being the first digital weapon to cause physical destruction. What real-world facility did it target?
options: A European hydroelectric dam
An Iranian nuclear enrichment facility
A German automotive factory
A Nordic power grid substation

easy.title: What is a Botnet?
easy.text: Many major European DDoS attacks rely on botnets. What is a botnet?
options: A network of infected 'zombie' computers controlled remotely by an attacker.
A secure firewall used by European banks.
An automated antivirus scanner.
A type of encrypted USB drive.

easy.title: The ILOVEYOU Worm (2000)
easy.text: The ILOVEYOU virus infected millions of computers across Europe and the world in hours. How did it primarily spread?
options: Through infected Bluetooth headphones.
Via an email attachment disguised as a love letter.
By exploiting smart TVs.
Through public Wi-Fi hotspots.

easy.title: European Data Protection
easy.text: Which landmark European Union regulation strictly governs how organizations collect and protect personal data like IP addresses and user profiles?
options: HIPAA
GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation)
CCPA
PCI-DSS

easy.title: Common Malware Entry Point
easy.text: According to ENISA (European Union Agency for Cybersecurity), what remains one of the most common initial ways malware enters an organization?
options: Satellite signal hijacking
Phishing emails with malicious links or attachments
Physical theft of server racks
Radio frequency jamming

medium.title: DNSChanger (2011 - Estonia)
medium.text: Created by the Estonian cybercrime ring 'Rove Digital', DNSChanger infected over 4 million PCs globally. What did it do?
options: It encrypted hard drives and demanded Bitcoin.
It hijacked victims' DNS settings to silently redirect web traffic to fraudulent ads and malicious sites.
It physically overheated laptop batteries.
It deleted the Windows operating system.

medium.title: WannaCry's Spreading Mechanism
medium.text: Which leaked Windows vulnerability allowed WannaCry to spread automatically like a worm across European corporate networks?
options: Heartbleed (OpenSSL)
Log4Shell (Java)
EternalBlue (SMBv1)
Spectre (CPU)

medium.title: NotPetya (2017 - Europe & Global)
medium.text: NotPetya spread via a compromised update of M.E.Doc software and paralyzed European shipping giant Maersk. Although it demanded a ransom, what was its true nature?
options: A destructive 'Wiper' that permanently destroyed the Master Boot Record (MBR) with no way to decrypt the data.
A cryptojacking worm mining Ethereum.
A harmless red-team test that escaped a lab.
A banking trojan stealing credit cards.

medium.title: Viasat / AcidRain (2022 - Europe)
medium.text: A 2022 wiper attack against the Viasat KA-SAT satellite network caused massive collateral damage in Central Europe. What physical infrastructure was affected?
options: Thousands of wind energy turbines in Germany lost remote control and monitoring.
Hydroelectric dam floodgates opened across Sweden.
Automated freight trains derailed in France.
Airport runways in Estonia lost lighting.

medium.title: Emotet (Europol Takedown 2021)
medium.text: Dismantled in 2021 by an international operation coordinated by Europol, how did Emotet evolve over time?
options: From a mobile game adware into a smart-TV virus.
From a banking trojan into a massive 'Malware-as-a-Service' botnet delivering ransomware.
From an antivirus into a firewall.
From a Linux kernel bug into a Wi-Fi cracker.

medium.title: The Mirai Botnet (2016)
medium.text: Mirai caused massive internet outages across Europe and the US. What type of devices did it primarily infect?
options: High-end gaming PCs.
IoT devices (IP cameras, routers, DVRs) using factory default usernames and passwords.
Apple iPhones via SMS.
Mainframe banking servers.

medium.title: Stopping WannaCry
medium.text: How did a British cybersecurity researcher accidentally halt the initial global spread of WannaCry?
options: By unplugging the main transatlantic fiber cable.
By registering an unregistered 'kill switch' domain hardcoded inside the malware.
By releasing a fake Bitcoin wallet.
By hacking into the attackers' command server and deleting it.

hard.title: Stuxnet's OT Sabotage
hard.text: Once inside the air-gapped OT network, how did Stuxnet physically destroy the centrifuges without alerting engineers?
options: It shut down the facility's main electrical transformer.
It modified Siemens S7 PLC code to alter centrifuge speeds while replaying normal recorded telemetry to hide alarms.
It encrypted the HMI touchscreens with ransomware.
It flooded the network with DDoS packets.

hard.title: Industroyer / CrashOverride (2016)
hard.text: During the 2016 Kyiv power grid attack, what technical capability made Industroyer unique in malware history?
options: It spoke native industrial control protocols (IEC 104, IEC 61850) to directly open substation circuit breakers.
It used AI to guess operator passwords in real time.
It injected firmware directly into communication satellites.
It spread exclusively through smart meters in residential homes.

hard.title: Triton / Trisis (2017)
hard.text: Triton crossed a critical red line by risking human lives in an industrial plant. What specific system did it compromise?
options: Triconex Safety Instrumented Systems (SIS), designed to safely shut down the plant during emergencies.
Water purification chemical dispensers.
Subsea gas pipeline pressure sensors.
Biosafety lab air filtration units.

hard.title: BlackEnergy 3 (2015)
hard.text: Considered the first confirmed cyberattack to cause a power outage, how did attackers using BlackEnergy 3 cut power to over 225,000 people?
options: By blowing up physical transformers with malware.
By hijacking HMI/SCADA workstations remotely to manually flip circuit breakers, then wiping systems with KillDisk.
By jamming GPS timing signals.
By cutting fiber-optic cables outside the plant.

hard.title: Havex (2014 - Europe)
hard.text: Targeting European energy and industrial companies, how did the Havex RAT map out victims' OT networks?
options: By scanning for OPC (OLE for Process Control) servers via trojanized ICS vendor software updates.
By cracking Wi-Fi WPA2 handshakes.
By intercepting unencrypted satellite telemetry.
By exploiting Bluetooth beacons on factory floors.

hard.title: Conficker's Evasion (2008)
hard.text: Conficker infected millions of machines across Europe, including government and military networks. What technique did it popularize to prevent defenders from blocking its Command & Control (C2) servers?
options: Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA) that generated hundreds of new potential C2 domains daily.
Hiding commands inside YouTube video comments.
Using quantum encryption.
Routing all traffic through Tor exit nodes.

hard.title: SolarWinds / SUNBURST (2020)
hard.text: Affecting major US and European organizations, how was the SUNBURST backdoor initially delivered to targets?
options: Via a zero-day exploit in Google Chrome.
Embedded inside a digitally signed, legitimate software update for the Orion IT monitoring platform (Supply Chain Attack).
Through infected USB sticks distributed at a Brussels summit.
Via compromised BGP routing tables.
